column4: The section's dictionary form for a great communal cauldron meets the Qur'an's “قُدُورٍ رَّاسِيَاتٍ” (fixed cauldrons); the same ayah asks David's household for grateful work, turning abundance into a received trust.

The section sets a shared meal against the Kenud who “eats alone”; this ayah has people give food to the needy, orphan, and captive while it is still loved (“عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِ”), reversing the closed hand.

The section's root حبّ depicts attachment to wealth; this ayah makes giving wealth “عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِ” part of righteousness, so love need not end in hoarding. The phrase can retain the sense of giving while the wealth is loved.
The section's root حبّ joins love to what one takes for good; “مِمَّا تُحِبُّونَ” says righteousness is not reached until some of what one loves is spent.

The section's dictionary reading of root ش د د is binding tightly, and its fist is gathered shut; this command names a hand bound to the neck (“مَغْلُولَةً إِلَىٰ عُنُقِكَ”), the bodily image of stinginess.
The section's dictionary gloss of شديد is بخيل; those who withhold (“بَخِلُوا”) what God gave will be made to wear it as a collar (“سَيُطَوَّقُونَ”), turning stinginess into a bodily bond.
The section's dictionary sense of جمع is drawing parts together; “وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰ” describes the person who gathers wealth and keeps it stored away, the same closed-fist action.
The section's root جمع is gathering things together; this ayah names the person who “جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ,” accumulating wealth and repeatedly counting it.
The section's root حبّ explains attachment that sticks; here people “تُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا,” a piled-up love of wealth, immediately beside neglect of others.
After neglecting the orphan and hungry, this passage says “تَأْكُلُونَ التُّرَاثَ أَكْلًا لَّمًّا”: consuming inheritance greedily reverses the section's meal prepared for guests and shared out.

The section says its dictionary sense of الخير is substantial wealth from a good source; this command to spend from good earnings (“مِن طَيِّبَاتِ مَا كَسَبْتُمْ”) forbids selecting the bad for others.
The section explicitly identifies its dictionary sense of الخير as wealth; this testamentary ayah uses “خَيْرًا” for what a person leaves and directs a bequest to parents and relatives.
The section gathers the shared table around a large pot and divided meat; here sacrificed camels provide food to eat and to give to the needy, joining provision to sharing.
The section's feast for an arriving traveler has a close ritual counterpart: this ayah tells pilgrims to eat sacrificial livestock and feed the distressed poor.

The section's dictionary image of the Kenud is one who eats alone and withholds help; the hosts here give others priority even when they themselves need the food, and are guarded from “شُحَّ نَفْسِهِ”.
The section's tight hand is stated directly: people would hold back from spending (“لَأَمْسَكْتُمْ”) for fear of depletion, and the ayah calls the human being “قَتُورًا”.
The section turns the collector's hand toward the final reckoning; here the collector falsely supposes that his wealth (“مَالَهُ”) will make him last forever (“أَخْلَدَهُ”).
The section's miser stores what could have become shared food; this ayah names those who hoard gold and silver (“يَكْنِزُونَ الذَّهَبَ وَالْفِضَّةَ”) and do not spend it for God.
The next ayah gives the hoard a bodily end: the gold and silver become the heated metal that brands their foreheads, sides, and backs, reversing secure storage into punishment.
The section's table opposes solitary eating; this ayah indicts the failure to honor the orphan (“لَّا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ”), naming one person the hoarder's closed hand leaves out.
The section puts a common pot and ladle against withheld help; this ayah asks why people do not urge one another to feed the poor (“طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ”).
The section's Kenud withholds aid; this ayah gives the specific failure, not urging the feeding of the poor (“لَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ”).
The section's description of the Kenud includes beating a dependent and withholding aid; this ayah depicts the person who rudely repels the orphan (“يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ”).
The section places a shared meal opposite solitary eating; here the condemned person does not encourage feeding the poor (“وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ”).
The section's Kenud “withholds his help”; this ayah says they withhold even the small customary aid (“وَيَمْنَعُونَ الْمَاعُونَ”).

This ayah describes the restless human (“هَلُوعًا”) whose pattern the next two verses specify: when hardship touches him he panics (70:20), but when good touches him he withholds (70:21); the section focuses on that latter response.

This is the other half of the pattern surrounding the section's cited 70:21: at hardship the human is “جَزُوعًا,” while 70:21 says he withholds when good reaches him. It distinguishes panic from the miser's response to having provision.
The section explicitly notes that here “الْخَيْرُ” is wealth and that the human is miserly; “وَإِذَا مَسَّهُ الْخَيْرُ مَنُوعًا” puts good and withholding together.

The section's common meal answers the hoarder's withholding; this passage says the just have a known right in their wealth (“فِي أَمْوَالِهِمْ حَقٌّ مَّعْلُومٌ”), which 70:25 identifies for the asker and deprived person.
This ayah names the recipients of the known wealth-right from 70:24, “لِلسَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ”; it makes the section's shared provision concrete.
The section identifies “خَيْر” as wealth; in this answer about what to spend, “مِنْ خَيْرٍ” is directed to parents, relatives, orphans, the poor, and travelers.
The section's meal and divided portions meet the harvest scene: eat the fruit when it bears and give its due on harvest day (“وَآتُوا حَقَّهُ يَوْمَ حَصَادِهِ”), without excess.
The section shows the fist closed around wealth; this command couples spending from what God provided with protection from the soul's greed (“شُحَّ نَفْسِهِ”), the reverse movement of the hand.
The hand image in 17:29 belongs to a passage about giving: this ayah assigns relatives, the needy, and travelers their due and warns against waste, setting both sides of the boundary.
Between the due to others in 17:26 and the bound hand in 17:29, this ayah warns that spendthrifts are brothers of devils; the shared meal must not become excess.

The section's wording رَبّ and خَبِير at 100:6,11 recurs here: after the hand-bound command in 17:29, this ayah says the Lord expands and restricts provision (“يَبْسُطُ الرِّزْقَ ... وَيَقْدِرُ”) and is fully aware of servants.
The section opposes a fist that will not open with a common table; this ayah places spending between waste and miserliness (“لَمْ يُسْرِفُوا وَلَمْ يَقْتُرُوا”), showing the measured boundary.
The section's dictionary gloss of شديد is بخيل; this ayah describes misers (“يَبْخَلُونَ”) who urge others to be miserly and conceal God's bounty (“وَيَكْتُمُونَ مَا آتَاهُمُ اللَّهُ”).
The section's dictionary gloss of شديد is بخيل; this ayah repeats that miserly word (“يَبْخَلُونَ”) and adds urging others to be miserly, extending the closed hand to a community.
Qarun's treasuries (“مِنَ الْكُنُوزِ”) and keys too heavy for a strong band of men give a concrete image of abundance accumulated, the section's “خَيْر” as much wealth turned into a burden.
Beside Qarun's treasure, this ayah directs him to seek the Hereafter with what God gave, do good as God has done good, and not spread corruption: wealth is judged by its use.
Qarun appears in full ornament before those who covet his worldly display; this gives a scene of wealth drawing desire, like the section's love that fixes on property.
The earth swallows Qarun and his house, and no group can rescue him; the fate reverses the security implied by hoarded treasure.
After Qarun's fall, those who wanted his position recognize that provision is expanded or restricted by God (“يَبْسُطُ الرِّزْقَ ... وَيَقْدِرُ”), not secured by wealth.
The section depicts clinging love of wealth; this begins the other path with giving (“أَعْطَىٰ”) and God-consciousness, directly reversing the tight hand.
The promise following the giving in 92:5–6 is that God will ease the giver toward ease (“فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ”), a reward against the collector's imagined security.
The section's dictionary gloss of شديد is بخيل; this ayah uses “بَخِلَ” for the direct opposite of the giver in 92:5, the closed hand at the section's shared table.
This ayah completes the withholding path: when the miser falls, his wealth (“مَالُهُ”) will not avail him, unlike the security he sought by keeping it.

The section calls good wealth that acquired from a praiseworthy way; this boundary forbids consuming one another's wealth unjustly (“بِالْبَاطِلِ”), distinguishing legitimate provision from wrongful gain.

The section's dictionary form describes wealth gathered by a praiseworthy means; this ayah prohibits wrongful consumption and allows trade by mutual consent (“تِجَارَةً عَن تَرَاضٍ”), clarifying that source.
This ayah says the graves are scattered (“بُعْثِرَتْ”), echoing the resurrection scene beside the section; 82:5 completes it by saying each soul knows what it sent ahead and left behind.
After the graves scatter in 82:4, this ayah says each soul learns what it sent ahead and left behind (“قَدَّمَتْ وَأَخَّرَتْ”), making stored deeds answerable.
The section turns the clenched hand into a person whose inner contents are gathered; “يَوْمَ تُبْلَى السَّرَائِرُ” likewise makes concealed inner realities manifest on the Day of reckoning.
The section says what is in the chests is gathered and the Lord is “خبير”; this ayah names what God knows there: “وَمَا تُخْفِي الصُّدُورُ,” what breasts conceal.
The section's hidden chest is made explicit here: people fold their breasts (“يَثْنُونَ صُدُورَهُمْ”) to conceal, while God knows what they hide and reveal.

The section's wording about collected chest-contents and the Lord as خبير points to what is hidden inside; this ayah specifies that he knows what their breasts conceal (“مَا تُكِنُّ صُدُورُهُمْ”) and disclose.
This repeated formulation says the Lord knows what breasts conceal and reveal (“مَا تُكِنُّ صُدُورُهُمْ”); it parallels the section's collected contents of the chest and divine knowledge.

The section's dictionary sense of نقيعة is food made for a traveler; Abraham's honored guests receive a fat calf (“بِعِجْلٍ سَمِينٍ”), a specific meal prepared for arrivals. Neighbor 51:27 shows him bring it near and invite them to eat.
The section's traveler's meal is echoed when Abraham brings food close to his arriving guests and asks them to eat (“فَقَرَّبَهُۥٓ إِلَيْهِمْ”); 51:26 identifies it as a fat calf.

A second telling of Abraham's guest scene serves a roasted calf (“بِعِجْلٍ حَنِيذٍ”); it recalls the section's dictionary form for a meal prepared for a traveler, though the Qur'an calls these guests rather than travelers.
The section shows wealth collected into a closed reserve; this parable pictures wealth spent for God as a grain multiplying into many ears, a different kind of increase than hoarding.
The section's fixation on “خَيْر” as property is bounded here: wealth and children are adornment of worldly life, while enduring good deeds (“وَالْبَاقِيَاتُ الصَّالِحَاتُ”) are better and last.
The section's collector attaches himself to immediate wealth before the final disclosure; this ayah names preferring the nearer life (“تُؤْثِرُونَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا”).
Against the section's apparent “خَيْر” of riches, this ayah calls the Hereafter better (“خَيْرٌ”) and more lasting (“أَبْقَىٰ”).
The section's love is attachment to what seems good; this ayah names the preference beneath it as love of the immediate life (“تُحِبُّونَ الْعَاجِلَةَ”).
The next ayah completes the contrast begun in 75:20 by saying people leave the Hereafter (“وَتَذَرُونَ الْآخِرَةَ”), the horizon against which the section's hoarding is judged.
This warning says wealth and children must not distract from remembrance (“لَا تُلْهِكُمْ أَمْوَالُكُمْ”); 63:10 then tells people to spend before death, making the danger of fixation concrete.
This ayah urges spending from God's provision before death arrives (“وَأَنفِقُوا مِمَّا رَزَقْنَاكُم”), the available moment for loosening the section's closed hand; 63:11 closes off delay.
This ayah states that no soul is delayed when its term comes (“وَلَن يُؤَخِّرَ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا”); it completes 63:10's urgency to give before death.
The section's dictionary sense of قَدْح includes an arrow used in maysir; this ayah prohibits using divining arrows (“بِالْأَزْلَامِ”), setting a boundary around taking shares by lot.

The section's arrow-and-share dictionary image meets the Qur'an's condemnation of maysir and arrows (“الْمَيْسِرُ وَالْأَزْلَامُ”); this is a contrary form of distributing a portion, not a communal meal.
The consequence for the withholding path of 92:8–9 is ease toward hardship (“فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ”), reversing the promise of ease to the giver in 92:7.

The section's dictionary definition of the fist uses تقبضها (closing the palm); this ayah says hypocrites “يَقْبِضُونَ أَيْدِيَهُمْ,” physically closing their hands and withholding, a direct opposite to the shared table.
The section's dictionary gloss of شديد is بخيل; when these people receive bounty, they “بَخِلُوا بِهِ” and turn away, making the closed hand a response to provision.
After the withholding in 9:76, this ayah says hypocrisy is left in their hearts (“نِفَاقًا فِي قُلُوبِهِمْ”) until they meet God; it gives the inward consequence beside the section's gathered chest.
This ayah gives the promise that precedes 9:76: if given bounty, they will give charity; 9:76 then shows the promise reversed once provision arrives.

After the people feed the needy and captive in 76:8, this ayah gives their stated motive: they feed solely for God (“لِوَجْهِ اللَّهِ”), wanting neither repayment nor thanks, unlike the wealth-lover's self-serving grip.

Under the wall of two orphans is a hidden treasure (“كَنزٌ لَّهُمَا”), preserved for them by their righteous father; the stored wealth is a deliberate provision for others, opposite the section's self-hoarder.
The section's shared table includes the orphan; this command requires handing orphans their property and forbids consuming it or exchanging the good for the bad (“وَلَا تَأْكُلُوا أَمْوَالَهُمْ”).
Where the section opposes solitary consumption and withholding, this ayah warns that consuming orphan property unjustly is like eating fire (“أَمْوَالَ الْيَتَامَىٰ ظُلْمًا”).
The section's common pot and divided portions oppose taking all for oneself; this ayah assigns a prescribed share in inheritance to both men and women, whether the estate is small or large.
At the division of an inheritance, this ayah directs that attending relatives, orphans, and the poor be given something from it; it makes the section's shared provision concrete at an estate.
This ayah bounds a guardian's use of orphan wealth: the rich must refrain from consuming it, while a poor guardian may take only fairly; the wealth is entrusted, not a private hoard.

This ayah distributes communal wealth to relatives, orphans, poor people, and travelers so it does not merely circulate among the rich (“كَيْ لَا يَكُونَ دُولَةً بَيْنَ الْأَغْنِيَاءِ”); it sets the section's shared-pot image against concentrated ownership.

This ayah assigns defined shares from gathered spoils to relatives, orphans, poor people, and travelers; its allocation of a common acquisition parallels the section's divided portions and shared food.
The section names الخير as wealth and also as generosity; for a debtor in hardship this ayah says to grant time, and that remitting the debt as charity is better (“وَأَن تَصَدَّقُوا خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ”).

The section binds the hand and later gathers what is inside; this ayah binds each person's record to their neck and brings it out open (“كِتَابًا يَلْقَاهُ مَنشُورًا”), making the bodily bond answerable at judgment.
After the open record in 17:13, this ayah commands each person to read their own book (“اقْرَأْ كِتَابَكَ”); it makes the disclosure personal, beside the section's account of inner contents.

Between giving others their due in 17:26 and the bound hand in 17:29, this ayah says that if one must turn a needy petitioner away while awaiting God's bounty, one should still speak gently; it separates inability to give from hardness.
The section's communal meal implies portions shared; this opening warning condemns short measure (“الْمُطَفِّفِينَ”), a reversal in which the giver of a portion cheats the receiver.
This ayah specifies that the short-measure takers demand full measure when receiving (“اكْتَالُوا عَلَى النَّاسِ”), the self-favoring share-taking that the section's common table resists.
The counterpart in this ayah is cheating people when weighing or measuring for them (“يُخْسِرُونَ”), completing the reversal of fair, divided provision.
The feeders in 76:8–9 say they fear a stern day (“نَخَافُ ... يَوْمًا عَبُوسًا”); this ayah supplies that motive, linking generosity with the section's resurrection reckoning.

After the passage's rebuke of neglecting the orphan and poor and loving wealth (89:17–20), this ayah voices regret: “يَا لَيْتَنِي قَدَّمْتُ لِحَيَاتِي”; it names what the hoarder wishes he had sent ahead.

This ayah identifies fear of poverty as a force against spending (“الشَّيْطَانُ يَعِدُكُمُ الْفَقْرَ”) and sets God's promise of bounty against it, sharpening the section's image of holding wealth from fear.
When the records are spread (“الصُّحُفُ نُشِرَتْ”), this ayah gives another disclosure scene beside the section's gathered chest; 81:14 says each soul then knows what it brought.
This ayah says every soul will know what it has brought (“مَا أَحْضَرَتْ”), making the deeds disclosed in 81:10 personal, as the section makes chest-contents answerable.

On the day all are raised, God informs them of what they did, having counted it while they forgot (“أَحْصَاهُ اللَّهُ وَنَسُوهُ”); divine accounting reverses the section's obsessive counting of wealth.
